definition: The number of protons in an atomic nucleus. It decides which element the atom is – all atoms with 6 protons are carbon.
The total number of protons and neutrons in a nucleus. The number of neutrons is the mass number minus the atomic number.
A version of an element. Isotopes of the same element have the same number of protons but different numbers of neutrons, e.g. carbon-12 and carbon-14.
A small 'packet' of electromagnetic radiation. An atom sends out a photon when an electron falls to a shell closer to the nucleus. The photon's energy decides the colour of the light.
Radiation such as radio waves, infrared, visible light, UV, X-rays and gamma rays. All kinds travel at the speed of light in a vacuum; shorter wavelength means more energy per photon.
Radiation with enough energy to knock electrons out of atoms and molecules, forming ions. It can damage DNA in the body's cells. Examples: alpha, beta, gamma and X-rays.
When unstable atomic nuclei break down by themselves and give off radiation. A substance with such nuclei is called radioactive.
Particle radiation of helium nuclei (2 protons and 2 neutrons) shot out from unstable nuclei. Stopped by a sheet of paper, but very harmful inside the body.
Electrons shot out from the nucleus when a neutron turns into a proton. The atomic number goes up by one. Stopped by a few millimetres of aluminium.
Very high-energy electromagnetic radiation given off by atomic nuclei. It does not change the number of protons or neutrons. Weakened by thick lead or concrete.
A chain of radioactive decays where each new nucleus is also unstable, until a stable nucleus forms. The uranium series produces radon, among others, and ends with lead.
The time it takes for half of the radioactive nuclei of an isotope to decay. After each half-life, half of what was left remains.
How many radioactive decays happen per second in a substance. Measured in becquerel (Bq): 1 Bq is one decay per second.
A measure of how much ionising radiation a person has received and how harmful it is. Measured in sievert (Sv), usually millisievert (mSv).
Nuclear splitting: a heavy nucleus, such as uranium-235, splits into two smaller ones when hit by a neutron. Energy and new neutrons are released.
When neutrons from one fission split new nuclei, which give more neutrons. In a nuclear power plant it is kept under control; in an atomic bomb it runs out of control.
When light nuclei join to form a heavier one, e.g. hydrogen to helium. Energy is released. Fusion is what gives the Sun its energy.
